title: How the Five Day Weekend Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the "Five Day Weekend" idea, a tongue-in-cheek marketing campaign by the Asheville Convention and Visitors Bureau and its Friends of the Five Day Weekend movement, which proposed a two-day work week and a constitutional amendment. They cover American overwork and job satisfaction statistics, unused vacation days, Parkinson's law, leisure time versus chores, health links to lack of vacation, and Keynes's 1930 prediction of a leisure society. They interview economists Robert Frank (Cornell) and Richard Freeman (Harvard) on why the prediction failed and what a two-day work week would do to the economy. The episode closes with listener mail about the Delta Force episode.
topics: Friends of the Five Day Weekend

entities.name: Friends of the Five Day Weekend

segments.title: Opening banter and the two-day work week
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck banter about Chuck's holiday time off and the idea of a two-day work week versus a five-day weekend.

segments.title: Origins of the Friends of the Five Day Weekend
segments.summary: The movement is introduced as a tongue-in-cheek marketing campaign by the Asheville Convention and Visitors Bureau, including a proposed constitutional amendment. Hosts note public response and Donald Trump's dismissal of the idea.
topics: Friends of the Five Day Weekend

segments.title: American overwork and job satisfaction statistics
segments.summary: Statistics are cited on job satisfaction from a 2007 Conference Board survey, the 2004 finding that a third of Americans feel overworked, and 2006 data on unused vacation days.

segments.title: History of the weekend and the Fair Labor Standards Act
segments.summary: The hosts say the weekend was created by Congress through the Fair Labor Standards Act, which established a 40-hour work week, minimum wage, and limits on child labor.

segments.title: Parkinson's law, leisure time, and health
segments.summary: Parkinson's law is discussed as a reason work might fit into fewer days. Leisure time is distinguished from chores, and a University of Pittsburgh and SUNY Oswego study linking vacation lack to heart disease risk is cited.

segments.title: European vacation norms
segments.summary: Chuck describes a British diplomat he met in Croatia who had 36 paid days off per year, a common standard in Europe.

segments.title: Keynes's leisure society prediction
segments.summary: Chuck explains Keynes's 1930 essay Economic Possibilities for Our Grandchildren, which predicted a leisure society within a century based on growth estimates, and notes that growth exceeded his predictions without the leisure society arriving.

segments.title: Expert interviews: Robert Frank and Richard Freeman
segments.summary: Robert Frank of Cornell argues relative needs grew, and Richard Freeman of Harvard says a five-day week is near optimal. Both had chapters in a book revisiting Keynes. Chuck gives his own view that four days would suit him.

segments.title: Economic effects of a two-day work week
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how a two-day week paid on production would shrink domestic wages and goods, raising prices of imported luxury goods, and that people would still compete for status goods.

segments.title: Listener mail on the Delta Force episode
segments.summary: Listener David criticizes the Delta Force episode for excessive admiration of special forces, and another listener asks for an episode on European special forces. The hosts respond.
